lesson.grammar_point: present perfect vs past simple for reporting a period

listenings.text: People ask me what I want from a regional report, and the honest answer is very simple. I want the headline in the first thirty seconds. Not the context, not the methodology, and please not an apology for the connection. The headline. Tell me the number, tell me whether it is good or bad, and then tell me why. I sit through eleven of these calls every quarter, and I can tell you that the directors I trust most are not the ones with the best English. They are the ones who know which number matters. If you open with fifteen slides of background, I stop listening and I start reading my email. And one more thing, because nobody says it out loud. Nobody on this call is a native speaker of English. I am Italian. Half the room speaks Spanish. If you wait until your English is perfect to speak with authority, you will wait forever.

When I moved from sales into a director role, the hardest part was not the strategy. It was the first ninety seconds of every presentation. I used to start with a long introduction because I was nervous, and the more nervous I was, the longer the introduction became. A colleague gave me a rule that changed everything, and I still use it today. One sentence for the headline, one sentence for the reason, and one sentence for what you want from the room. Thirty seconds, and then you can go into the detail. The other thing I learned is to flag the bad news myself, early, before anyone asks for it. If the loss ratio has gone up, I say it in the first minute. Nobody has ever been fired for saying it early. People do get into trouble for letting the number appear on slide fourteen.

extra_audio.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I will walk you through the third quarter in three parts. The headline figure is that we have grown eleven percent year on year. The main driver was the corporate portfolio in the south. What I need from you today is a decision on our exposure to climate risk.
